newsitem.title: USA: Tight U.S. security on Waco, Oklahoma anniversaries.
newsitem.headline: Tight U.S. security on Waco, Oklahoma anniversaries.

text.p: Security has been beefed up at federal buildings to guard against possible extremist attacks on Saturday's twin anniversary of the Oklahoma City bombing and FBI raid on the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas.

At courthouses, military installations, FBI offices and even historic monuments across the country, new measures were implemented this week to prevent attacks from anti-government militias or lone bombers.

"These people look for a weak spot so we can't afford to ease up anywhere. We have to protect every building, every courthouse," U.S. Marshal D.B. Bransom, in charge of security arrangements in northern Texas, said on Friday.

The security measures ranged from installing barricades on streets outside federal buildings to simply closing all Venetian blinds in order to protect against flying glass in any bomb attack. Extra security guards and metal detectors were also deployed at many buildings.

With April 19 seen by anti-government groups as a memorial day for their "martyrs," the Federal Bureau of Investigation has issued an advisory warning to other federal government agencies and to state and local law enforcement agencies.

Officials stressed they were not aware of any specific, credible threats of terrorist acts planned for this weekend but nevertheless were prepared for the worst. "Every year around this time, we remind people of the significance of that date and to take security precautions," an FBI spokesman said.

On April 19, 1993, Branch Davidian cult leader David Koresh and about 80 of his followers were killed by flames or gunfire when the FBI raided their compound at the end of a 51-day standoff. Federal officials said cult members started the fire themselves but anti-government groups blamed the FBI, and Waco quickly became a rallying cry of the extreme right.
Dozens of militia members were to attend a memorial service on Saturday at the site of the Davidians' compound, now no more than a few concrete ruins and burned-out cars.

Exactly two years after the Branch Davidian fire, 168 people were killed when a huge truck bomb blew apart the federal government building in downtown Oklahoma City. Prosecutors allege that Timothy McVeigh, who is currently on trial in Denver, planted the bomb in revenge for Waco.

Security has been tight since the start of McVeigh's trial but nerves were further rattled by wild rumours that the pilot of an A-10 attack plane loaded with four bombs, which disappeared on April 2, may have landed at a remote Colorado airfield and be planning to bomb the Denver courthouse.

Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said on Thursday there was no evidence to connect the plane's disappearance to the McVeigh trial. But he said military bases had been ordered to tighten security ahead of Saturday's anniversary.

Federal officials said they have one advantage in preparing for April 19 this year: it falls on a Saturday, so most government buildings will be closed. Still, post offices will be open and increased surveillance is expected at airports and historic monuments.

A spokesman for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which oversees LaGuardia, Kennedy and Newark airports, said its police have "been advised to be extra vigilant" and agents at the Capitol building in Washington said they would have additional officers on patrol this weekend.
"The buildings are open and we urge people to come on up. But they will see more uniformed police officers," Capitol Police spokesman Sgt. Dan Nichols said.

"We have three reasons for that -- to serve as a deterrent, to more closely monitor vehicle traffic and, just as important, it reassures the visiting public that we have taken added precautions to protect their safety and security."
While some federal workers said they appreciated the extra security effort in the days leading up to April 19, other members of the public were less impressed.

"I'm not worried about anything, its a lot of hyperbole. There are a lot of very paranoid people here," said Paul Fisher, a Dallas engineer on jury duty, as he entered the federal courthouse in downtown Dallas on Friday.
